question: Which bits does the description of the TrueHD bitstream reserve, does any real stream set one, and does this decoder ignore them as the description says a parser should?
method: Section 3.2 of the high-level bitstream description: "reserved bitfields are encoded as v(n) and should be ignored by parsers". The reserved fields a major sync and a restart header have are counted by the census of `verify --census`: sixteen bits of the major sync, two of `format_info`, two before `extended_substream_info`, the two low ones of `substream_info`, two of the channel meaning; two of the restart header, the bit of a heavy dynamic range control the major sync does not announce, and the twelve where its update would stand. Three rules file a bit that is set, at `info`. The census was added up over the streams of the corpus and over the first minute of every TrueHD and MLP track of a library. Then nine copies of the fixture were made, each with one of these bits set in its first access unit and the checksums over it recomputed, and put to the binary of main, the binary of the change, and three other decoders as black boxes: a stream in, samples out. The streams of the corpus and the library are media and are not in the repository; the nine copies are made from the fixture.

reading: No real stream sets one: not one of 71916 major syncs and 282184 restart headers of the corpus, nor of 92101 and 340180 of the library, has a reserved bit set, so the three rules have never fired on a real stream. Two bits the syntax calls reserved are no rule, because encoders set them all the time: the reserved bit of a directory entry and `hires_output_timing`. And this decoder did not ignore every reserved bit: a major sync that differed from the first in one of `format_info`, of the two before `extended_substream_info` or of `substream_info` was a change of configuration to `verify`, and the last of them stopped the decode. The Dolby decoder and FFmpeg play all nine copies as they play the fixture, and so does the change.
